summary_clean: Chennai resident Seshadri Sukumar kickstarted a career in sports photography, mid-life, turning his back on the familiar and the comfortable, including a long career in the banking sector, and that has made all the difference. He is right now covering the 20th Asian Games in Japan
body_clean: In cricket, one regularly comes across teams that shift to a whole new lane in the second innings, with surprising progress, eclipsing their first-innings performance. And in that process, they bring immense joy and wonder to spectators. Seshadri Sukumar has pulled off something similar to that. Here are the details of 71-year-old Seshadri’s second innings: a Press Information Bureau-accredited international sports photographer from Chennai and a Canon EOS Ambassador. He now has a reputation for “checking into” major international sporting events. As this article is being written, he is shooting images of sporting excellence at the 20th Asian Games, unfolding at Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya in Japan. Before zooming in on what he is doing now, a quick run of his first innings: Sukumar had been working in the banking sector, being an official photographer with Indian Overseas Bank (IOB). He always had an intense desire to be a sports photographer, but that remained a desire for a drearily long time. When retirement from his corporate career was looming large, Sukumar took the plunge and started pursuing sports photography full steam ahead. After Sukumar had been years into sports photography, in 2021, Sukumar’s nephew shared a story about his uncle’s passion for sports photography online. Sukumar was 66 years old then and covering the Tokyo Olympic Games. And the story of how someone is flourishing in a career kickstarted mid-life caught the world’s imagination. Sukuamar’s portfolio includes multiple Olympic Games, FIFA World Cups (including the most recent edition), ICC World Cups, Grand Slam tournaments, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, NBA events, FINA World Championships, FIDE World Cups and MotoGP, among several other major sporting events. Among his iconic photographs is one of the Rio Olympics, one that captured the contrasting emotions of the winner and the loser; the photograph won him a gold medal from the Photographic Society of America (PSA). Sukumar’s professional photographs have been distributed through international wire services and stock photography libraries, including Alamy, Zuma Press, IMAGO Images, SOPA Images and Reuters Connect. Sukumar’s life and career are a reminder that it is never too late to start afresh. Published - October 04, 2026 09:52 am IST

title: A hobby evolves to meet Gen Zers on their terms
title_clean: A hobby evolves to meet Gen Zers on their terms
title_normalized: a hobby evolves to meet gen zers on their terms
summary_clean: Advances in technology, easier licensing procedures and affordability are among the factors that make amateur radio attractive to youngsters, even those still in school. Here are perspectives of amateur radio enthusiasts and a seller of hobby-related equipment from Chennai
body_clean: There is usually an apocalyptic air to how Ham radio is perceived. The Ham radio enthusiast is readily visualised as trudging into a land overtaken by a massive disaster and where all technology-based communication lines outside the amateur-radio sphere have broken down. The enthusiast has morphed into a saviour, connecting with a fellow hobbyist elsewhere in the “universe” and communicating a local situation, dire and distressing, amidst the static and crackle of radio communication, to reach help to the suffering. This description is indeed fact-aligned. Ham radio enthusiasts do take centre stage during disasters. One witnessed that during the Kerala floods of 2018 and closer home, in the harrowing first week of December 2015 in Chennai. But distress communication is only one of the things riding on amateur radio airwaves. Net sessions (as on-air meetups of Ham radio hobbyists are known) are also defined by banter, in fact, more by small talk than SOS calls. And do not be surprised if the banter is punctuated with Gen Z lingo. N. Deepan (call sign VU2DPN), a key member of the Madras Amatuer Radio Society (MARS), points out that the Ham radio hobby has never been as accessible to youngsters as it is now. From licensing to practising the hobby, the procedures of initiation and the operation of the equipment have become ridiculously simple. Having seen 63 summers and getting started on the hobby around four decades ago, Deepan is at a vantage point to talk about the hobby’s evolution. The Wireless Planning and Coordination wing (WPC) is responsible for conducting Amateur Station Operator’s Certificate (ASOC) examinations and issuing the license. Deepan underlines the examinations have become simpler as technology has organically taken certain “subjects” off the table. And the removal of this barrier encourages the entry of youngsters. Anyone aged 12 and above can appear for the exam and get the license. “Where it took one or two years to get a license, it takes approximately one month,” observes Deepan, noting that objective questions have replaced the earlier pattern of examination. And the new license holder can hit the ground running, the process of getting started on the hobby also having become facile. EchoLink, Z3 DMR, and Droidstar allow licensed operators to communicate using just a phone with other amateur radio enthusiasts. Once the license is validated, usually within 24 hours, the software can be used. And that obviates the need to invest in ham radio equipment; that can wait. Deepan has seen the ham radio equipment move from valves to transistors, ICs and now Software Defined Radio (SDR). With advancing technology, the equipment has shrunk, and so has their prices. Deepan attributes the fall in prices to the shift from imported equipment to local dealerships (to sell ham radio equipment, a dealer’s license is required). That brings us to someone like Gaurav Srivatsava and his wife Shivangi Gaurav, both ham radio license holders and diehard enthusiasts, and beyond that, owners of Radio Brewery in Iyyapanthangal (radiobrewery.com), which sells amatuer radio equipment. Shivangi largely manages the business while Gaurav continues to work in the IT sector. Their own personal struggles in finding reliable and cost-effective equipment locally had crystallised into this business venture in 2018. Gaurav recalls that besides importing, Ham radio enthusiasts in Chennai were dependent on a couple of dealers in Delhi. The hobbyists would together buy in bulk to keep prices within their comfort range. Among those who encouraged them to start this business was Deepan, one of Gaurav’s mentors and supporters. Among factors that augur well for the hobby, Gaurav says, is the portability of the ham radio gear. He recalls the time when valve radios, measuring six by six feet, “appropriated” a room in exchange for the joy of communicating on amateur radio airwaves. Fast forward to now, low-powered ham radio equipment can “fit into a small bread box”. Deepan notes that even if one were to route their ham radio communication through an amateur radio satellite, the allied equipment, which includes SDR dongle, dish antenna and up converter or transverter, is easy on the back, being eminently portable. Both Deepan and Gaurav have noticed youngsters taking to the hobby. Gaurav points out his daughter Pari Gaurav (VI2JXB/ KN6GRI, US amateur radio identifier ID), 19 years old now, cleared the WPC examination at age 12. Deepan’s daughter, Malini D. (VU3JJT) is also an avid ham radio enthusiast. Even youngsters without any precedent of ham radio engagement in their families are gravitating towards the hobby for the doors of communication it opens in various parts of the world. Deepan notes, “On the Net, all radio ham hobbyists connect and converse as equals.” To sum up, this hobby seems to have been made for Gen Zers (and the ones following them too) for two reasons. It is a generation that derives its strength and purpose from communication, even with those they will never meet in real life, and this hobby is geared to that. And two, this generation thrives on volunteering, and this hobby can provide opportunities for that during extremely harrowing times. title: Chennai’s monsoon test
title_clean: Chennai’s monsoon test
title_normalized: chennai s monsoon test
summary_clean: This year, the IMD has predicted normal Northeast monsoon rainfall, with a strong El Niño likely to strengthen it further towards the end of the year. Is the new TVK government prepared to face the monsoon, or will Chennai have to brace for another deluge?
body_clean: Call it the continuum or an early image-building exercise, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who also holds the Municipal Administration portfolio, has already deployed Ministers and senior officials to take up flood-mitigation works well ahead of the onset of the Northeast monsoon. He has instructed that all de-silting and stormwater drain (SWD) works be completed as early as possible. Official data shows that the flood-vulnerable locations within the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) have dropped from nearly 800 in 2015 to 389 in 2023. The figure is 219 for the 2026 Northeast monsoon. The list of vulnerable locations is being continuously reviewed based on field-level assessments, rainfall patterns, and the effectiveness of the completed flood-mitigation works, said GCC officials. The micro-level SWD works are 95% complete, but there are severe capacity constraints along the Buckingham Canal, Adyar, and Sholinganallur, officials added. GCC Commissioner G.S Sameeran said the civic body is coordinating with the Railways, Chennai Metro Rail Limited, and other agencies on drainage and flood-mitigation works. “Some major infrastructure works may take longer. The GCC has implemented temporary solutions, such as pumping facilities, for managing the monsoon,” he said. Lack of consultation Mr. Sameeran and his team have been on routine inspections – almost daily – of various works across the city. Even so, there has been talk about a lack of consultation and transparency in the conduct of flood-mitigation works. MDMK councillor S. Jeevan of Ward 35 in Perambur said, “Elected representatives do not know what is happening during flood preparedness inspections. I have not been able to meet the assistant engineer for 10 days to discuss residents’ complaints. The flood risk is high this year due to delays in desilting canals such as the Kodungaiyur Canal.” Federation of North Chennai Residents Welfare Association president T. Shanmugam said residents were worried as officials had not shared details of flood preparedness yet. Haris Sulthan, an activist in Padi, said most waterbodies in and around Chennai and its suburbs remained largely dry, with the five drinking water reservoirs together holding 4.5 TMC against the 11.7 TMC total capacity. He said routine annual works were being carried out, but no new major flood-mitigation interventions had been undertaken beyond these works in many areas, including Medavakkam, Chitlapakkam, Hasthinapuram, Kadaperi, Ambedkar Road, Jothi Nagar, and Sunnambu Kolathur, where prolonged inundation was reported previously. He appreciated the cancellation/reversal of tenders of “cosmetical lake-front development” works by the newly elected TVK government, while also calling for further desilting, the removal of water hyacinth, and increasing the lake depth. Urbanisation challenge According to a senior official in the GCC, Chennai’s monsoon vulnerability, particularly in the south of the city, is largely due to unchecked urbanisation, and that flooding in many parts like near Perumbakkam is “100% man-made”. Pointing to the built-up spaces and encroachments around the Pallikaranai marshland, Perungudi, and the IT corridor, he said that natural watercourses are choked, and canals in T. Nagar and Mambalam are heavily polluted because the “entire waterway is a sewer due to illegal sewage connections.” K.P. Subramanian, an urban planner, highlighted that while flood resilience in Velachery has improved, areas like Kuber Nagar, Karthikeyapuram, and parts of Madipakkam still face risks due to urban development and drain silting. He recommends regular desilting and zoning regulations to designate flood plains, rivers, and lake margins as no-development zones. D. Raghunandan, a climate researcher at Delhi Science Forum, said the SWD network in Chennai and its suburbs must be redesigned to handle extreme rainfall events such as 100-200 mm or more in just a few hours, rather than just evenly distributed volumes of rain. Instead of a haphazard pattern of urbanisation, the buildings, roads, and flyovers must be planned to ensure natural drainage and that the connectivity of stormwater drains to the three major rivers running through the city, and eventually into the sea, is not affected. Chennai must protect its wetlands and lakes, such as in Perumbakkam and Pallikaranai; the depth of the Cooum and Adyar rivers has also reduced compared to yesteryears. Increasing the capacity of waterbodies would help store excess rainfall water or drain it naturally towards the sea, he suggested. “These are long and costly overhaul processes that have to be addressed systematically over time, but they would pay back by offsetting losses during frequent urban floods,” he noted, adding that similar measures were needed in all major cities, not just in Chennai. S. Janakarajan, president of the South Asia Consortium for Interdisciplinary Water Resources Studies and former professor at MIDS, said water conservation must be prioritised since short, heavy downpours are the new normal. He said 70% to 80% of rainfall runs off into the sea because departments uncoordinatedly drain water, and suggested that the State focus on conservation to mitigate floods and droughts. “There are 4,100 lakes in the three adjoining districts [Tiruvallur, Chengalpattu, and Kancheepuram], besides numerous temple tanks and ponds that can help augment surface water and improve groundwater recharge. Also, temporary holding ponds could be created in educational institutions, parks, playfields, and government land, while large private land parcels could also be considered for creating sponge parks,” he said. Monsoon preparedness The WRD, meanwhile, is set to complete the first phase of its annual desilting exercise in a week. However, vast swathes of water hyacinth hindering the free flow of floodwater in waterways remain a challenge this year, too. While the department has accelerated work to clean the major and minor waterways ahead of the Northeast monsoon, residents of various parts of the city have urged the authorities to coordinate with other agencies to prevent sewage from entering the waterways. The department has deployed about 400 machines, including floating excavators, to clean the waterways, including the Adyar, Cooum, Kosasthalaiyar, and Araniyar rivers, as well as the Buckingham canal, and also clear sand bars at the various river mouths. Officials noted that the ₹42-crore project would help minimise flooding in the rivers and backflow into micro drains by 70% to 80% during the monsoon. The rivers would be able to handle the flows without spillover, even in the event of 200 mm of rainfall in a day. Sewer networks To reduce sewage-related complaints during the ensuing Northeast monsoon, Chennai Metro Water has completed the second phase of cleaning the city’s sewer network. The network was cleaned through 41,996 manholes during this phase, carried out between July and September. As floodwater often enters the sewer network during heavy rain, the water agency plans to undertake a third phase of cleaning between October and December to minimise blockages and prevent sewer network failures, officials said. Nearly 417 sewage pumping stations and sewage treatment plants have been equipped with IoT-based monitoring systems to help detect and prevent sewage stagnation and overflows. Robotic equipment is also being used to detect leaks and damages in drinking water pipelines. Power infrastructure The Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) covers flood mitigation works under 22 categories. The monsoon preparatory works are carried out on a massive scale this year, a senior official of the TNPDCL said. Tree branch clearance was completed at 6.75 lakh locations, exposed underground cables were buried at 1,762 places, damaged insulators were replaced at 85,000 locations, and low-sag overhead lines were rectified at 54,387 places. Maintenance is under way at 2,650 substations and 3,840 pillar boxes. The TNPDCL is also replacing 40,000 damaged concrete poles and worn-out conductors at 2,500 locations. Distribution transformer structures are maintained at 60,000 places, according to data shared by the TNPDCL. Maintenance works are nearly complete across distribution regions, barring Chennai North, Central, West, and South-I. Over 90% of monsoon preparatory works are done in Chennai South-II, Kancheepuram, and Tiruvallur, data showed. Works are expedited in central Chennai (T. Nagar, Anna Salai, Teynampet, Royapettah, Triplicane, and Mylapore), where only 52% of the works have been completed. In the western region covering Ambattur, Avadi, Maduravoyal, Anna Nagar, and Kolathur, 56% of the works are complete. ‘Early preparedness is key’ “Local bodies across Tamil Nadu have been directed to complete monsoon works by October 10. In Chennai, desilting has been under way for two and a half months, with one cycle covering nearly one lakh silt catch pits having been completed. The second cycle is under way. Similar instructions have been issued to other corporations, municipalities, and town panchayats,” said Municipal Administration and Water Supply (MAWS) Department Secretary Gagandeep Singh Bedi. “Very high rainfall in short duration and rainwater inflow from adjoining suburban areas would place more pressure on the SWD systems, so early preparedness is key,” he told the department heads at a recent meeting. (With inputs from K. Lakshmi, R. Srikanth, and Aloysius Xavier Lopez) Published - October 03, 2026 08:00 pm IST

body_clean: The ongoing dredging and bund work for the proposed Mamallan reservoir in the Kovalam-Nemmeli backwaters has affected a crucial habitat for migratory waterbirds, according to the Palluyir Trust for Nature Education and Research. In a representation to the Water Resources Department (WRD), the trust said four naturalists and zoologists surveyed the project area on September 29 and recorded around 3,500 waterbirds. The team recorded 51 species, including 25 migratory species protected under the UN Convention on Migratory Species. More than 1,500 garganey ducks, which migrate from temperate regions including Russia and Mongolia, were recorded foraging within the project site. More than 700 greater flamingos were also seen. Stopover site The trust said the Kovalam-Nemmeli wetland was an important stopover site for migratory birds arriving along the Central Asian Flyway during the August - September migration season. It said the presence of thousands of foraging birds indicated that the area comprised biologically active mudflats, although this had not been recognised in the coastal zone management plan. According to the trust, dredging and bunding for the reservoir had removed brackish and halophytic vegetation that had previously provided a buffer between waterbirds and traffic and human activity. Blocking tidal flow The blocking of tidal flow could also affect the movement of marine organisms during high tide and reduce prey availability for waterbirds, the trust said. The organisation also raised concerns about the project’s potential implications for flood drainage in south Chennai. Citing warnings by scientists from Anna University’s Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management about extreme weather and the possibility of severe cyclonic events in the Bay of Bengal, it said blocking a crucial flood channel could increase flood risks in the region around OMR. title: New RWA in Tambaram seeks review of property tax

summary_clean: Judge Colony and Neighbourhood Welfare Association raises concerns over drainage, groundwater contamination and road safety
body_clean: The newly formed Judge Colony and Neighbourhood Welfare Association, an initiative of the United Federation of Residents Welfare Associations in Tambaram City Corporation, has raised concerns over high property tax rates, groundwater contamination, inadequate drainage, poor roads and road safety. The association was formally inaugurated on September 27 in the presence of more than 100 residents. It has also submitted a memorandum to the Chief Minister’s Special Cell and the Municipal Administration and Water Supply Department (MAWS) seeking action on the issues. Property tax burden One of the major issues raised by the association was the property tax rates in Tambaram Corporation. S.M. Govindarajan, social activist, said the property tax revised by the Corporation in 2024 was significantly higher than that in several premium localities in Greater Chennai. According to Govindarajan, the property tax for a 1,500 sq ft residential building in Zone A of Tambaram Corporation was ₹26,812.65, which he said was 65% higher than the tax for a comparable property on Boat Club Road and 164% higher than that on North Usman Road, despite the latter having a lower guideline value. He said Chitlapakkam residents were facing a disproportionately high property tax burden despite relatively lower guideline values. He also said that, as per local body norms, an Appeals Committee comprising the Mayor/Commissioner and councillors, irrespective of political affiliation, should be in place. “There is no information on this and there was no public consultation or discussion among councillors before revising the tax rates,” he said. “Despite writing to Tambaram Corporation on this issue, zero action has been taken to date. Residents are forced to face a second property tax hike of 178%–550%, well above the 25%–100% ceiling fixed by the MAWS in G.O. 52 of March 2022,” he said. The association said it hoped for a positive response to its memorandum. Till then, it urged the Corporation to refrain from fixing a deadline for payment of the revised property tax. Civic and safety concerns Residents of Sriram Colony expressed concern over possible groundwater contamination by septic water and persistent drainage problems. According to Govindarajan, streets in Sriram Colony, in Ward 34, Zone 3, Tambaram Sanatorium, were flooded even during gentle downpours. As the area was low-lying and lacked stormwater drains, inundation during the rainy season posed serious problems. Residents also raised concerns over public safety near Krishnan Kovil and Thozhi Hostel, particularly after street lights were switched off. The association decided to take up the issue with the authorities and seek measures to improve street lighting and public safety. The poor condition of Chitlapakkam Main Road, a bus route and a State highway, and the Krishnan Kovil junction was another concern. Residents said uneven patches of concrete blocks and potholes posed a threat to motorists, particularly during peak hours. The association said it was surprised to receive a response from the Corporation Commissioner that the road would be re-laid “within three months” after the issue was raised. Residents also sought modification of the unusually high speed-breakers near a government school, saying they did not conform to Indian Roads Congress norms. They suggested reflective paint or markings to improve visibility at night. Activists also pointed to the death of a 34-year-old motorist in Chitlapakkam in 2024 in connection with an unmarked speed-breaker, and alleged that road safety norms continued to be flouted. summary_clean: From handrails in an apartment complex to a pool lift, here are some examples of how a little initiative can transform everyday living for senior citizens and those with special needs
body_clean: How accessible is your apartment community? That’s the central idea of this short film Block A For Accessibility, released with a private screening at PVR Satyam Cinemas on September 25. The 20-minute CBFC-certified film by YWTC (Yes, We Too Can!!!) Charitable Trust, in collaboration with Fiserv and United Way Mumbai as the CSR partner, is a story of care, community, and design. The film revolves around Natarajan, an ageing father, who after starting to use a wheelchair keeps himself isolated from the vibrant life of his apartment complex because he does not want to trouble his son. A sudden accident at the building’s stairs becomes a turning point for the entire community. The film follows the internal realisation of the association secretary and the decisive action of the builder. Natarajan’s character is played by a deaf person, Ravi Kumar. Voice was given by Umapathy, a wheelchair user. Most of the cast and crew are persons with disabilities, including the director. The film has sign language interpretations along with subtitles. The film addresses a universal civic necessity: accessible housing that accommodates an ageing population and ensures people of all abilities live with independence and dignity. Nonagenarian Arjun Krishna and Vasantha Arjun were too modest to talk about this accessibility feature and agreed to give their names after much prodding by this journalist. One of the earliest residents of this gated community, when the couple were part of the resident association, they got handrails fixed at most of the blocks some 20 years ago. These have been patronised by all, especially the senior citizens. But the community could do with some more, and the couple themselves have experienced the practical difficulty in not having them. “One of the ladies has even fallen not having a railing to hold on to it,” says Vasantha. The couple sponsored the entire cost of installing the handrailings at some new locations as a gift to the community that has been their home for the last 25 years (the couple marked 25 years of staying in the community this June). Pool lift: for easy swimming Madhavi Latha Prathigudupu’s day is not complete without accessing the swimming pool at her gated community in Arumbakkam. Since 2022, what makes this common amenity accessible for this para-athlete is the pool lift that was incorporated. The swimming champion cannot do without being in the pool and her late father had to help her get into the waters. She convinced Triumph Apartments, a community with 108 flats where she owns one, to make the pool accessible. “Before installing the pool lift, we had a demonstration done by the manufacturer with the committee members to get their approval,” says Madhavi, president of YWTC Charitable Trust. Today, she goes independently into the pool (she controls the lift pool through a remote) and most importantly has raised the importance of having inclusive amenities at gated communities not just for those with disabilities but even for use by the elderly. There was no ramp when she moved in to the community; the association did not just construct one for access to her block but made the improvisation at other towers as well. Accessibility standards of the National Building Code insist on a barrier-free built environment and all common facilities accessible to all people. “It’s your right, so ask the builder for such accessible features before investing in a flat,” she adds. summary_clean: At Artiform, Mylapore, the exhibition brings together artists Kannan P, Mani Murugesan, Ramki Ravi, Ramesh N, Surya S, and Yogeshwaran V who explores how wood, metal, graphite, and paper become materials for storytelling
body_clean: Our understanding of the world around us is constantly shaped by the materials that fill it. For artists, this relationship can become part of the creative process. In Material Memoir, a new show at Artiform, Mylapore, substances like wood, metal, and graphite, move beyond their physical forms to become ways of telling stories. Carved, layered, cut, shaped, each material gradually becomes a part of a narrative. The audience is left to wonder whether materials can indeed remember. The exhibition brings together the works of upcoming Chennai-based artists Kannan P, Mani Murugesan, Ramki Ravi, Ramesh N, Surya S and Yogeshwaran V. Some pieces quickly announce the idea of contemplating material memory and the central nature of life through indents, and suspension. There are some others that show you the palpable changes taking place in Nature through nests and webs. Take Kannan’s practice, for instance. He evidently engages with welding, sheet metal, wood, and bronze. Welding is central to his visual language. One of his pieces titled Metallic Nest: Solitude and Synergy, made entirely with steel, is inspired by the “collective architecture of the wasp’s nest,” says Kannan. Growing up in Chennai’s Ambattur, the presence of a wasp’s nest is something that he witnessed often. “A single paper wasp or honeybee cannot build a hive alone, yet together they craft complex structures through collective labour. In my practice and in life, I believe true strength and beauty emerge not from isolated creation, but from shared unity,” says Kannan. “Every time I clean a spider’s web in my house, it rebuilds again and again. Watching this cycle sparked a deep personal realisation. No matter how many times its creation is disrupted, the spider stays focussed solely on its work. For me, this only means that I need to keep moving forward despite every obstacle or setback. That is what I have tried to do in Perseverance,” he adds. Kannan says that the way he has used steel to construct a suspended human takes the form of a spider’s home and its infinite web. The piece, an already striking visual, hence becomes that much more compelling. “We think of wood, graphite, paper, metal, and all these materials as just something that is used to create an artwork. But when you actually look closely, they are not just materials. That is where the story begins. Each artist has approached the material in a different way, and even though their styles are distinctive, the material they have used carries an evocation,” says curator Isaiarasi Annamalai. Forms of Nature There are other artists who seem to be gravitating towards hymenoptera, arachnids, and other small creatures. Artist Ramki Ravi transforms paper through cutting, carving, and layering, challenging the material’s inherent flatness. Inspired by the forms of Nature, the sculpted pieces draw upon forms such as ‘honeycombs, fingerprints, and patterns of insect movement.’ The first work that catches your eye is titled Apian Society, made with paper and gold foil texture paste. The artwork is in all shades of orange and bright yellow; in some ways, it also reminds me of the golden hour evenings. The artist says that this artwork explores collective living through a honeycomb structure, highlighting how individual contributions create a harmonious society without rivalry or envy. Another work that catches my attention is titled Constellation, made with acrylic on canvas; the work resembles a starry night, a rare occurance for city dwelling people. For the artist, it denotes the endless thoughts that inhabit a human mind. “From waking to sleeping, the flow of thoughts appearing and disappearing resembles a starry night sky, expressing the ceaseless flux and energy of countless thoughts,” says Ramki. For artist Ramesh, much of his works draw inspiration from his recent travels to Kochi in Kerala. He uses etching, woodcut, and mixed media to show crabs, boats, and the shore as recurring themes. In one work, dense tree roots envelop the boats, while in another, a school of fish swims alongside them. All these paintings seem to inherently carry forward a philosophy of mushrooming from one’s roots. How this expounds, measures their success. Internal voice The exhibition also brings to us many external philosophies. Born in Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, artist Surya S was raised in a village environment, which shaped his sensitivity to everyday life. His work General Perspective, made with a mixed media of paper, wood, and steel, resembles a pinball game with its metallic balls of varying sizes. But the artist says, “the things we witness, learn, accept, and question gradually shape our sense of identity and belonging. What begins as an external influence eventually becomes an internal voice.” Another artist who seems to contemplate the world as a whole is Murugesan. His works draw on scientific thought, philosophical enquiry, and close observations of Nature, ideas that are also echoed in their titles, such as Dialectics, Primary Energy, and Inter+Outer+Infinite. In Dialectics, made with graphite on paper, the artwork calls for multiple observations. Call it an optical illusion; the work seems to reveal itself differently every time, making it an object of intrigue. Yogeshwaran on the other hand, explores human emotion, resilience, strength, and the expressive possibilities of form. He transforms industrial materials like bronze, steel, and iron into forms that appear to float, rotate, or move through space. In one of his works, Midday Night, made with cotton steel, the sculpture captures a moment of celestial eclipse. “The spiralling, concentric metal bands represent the orbital motion of the cosmos, while the two polished central spheres embody the sun and moon becoming one,” he says. With Kannan’s steel work, Ramki Ravi’s paper work, Ramesh N’s woodcuts and etchings, Surya S’s mixed-media works, Mani Murugesan’s graphite explorations and Yogeshwaran V’s sculptures, the exhibition looks at material not merely as a medium, but as a carrier of memory, observation, and experience. Across these practices, materials are cut, layered, welded, etched and shaped, taking on meanings that extend beyond their physical qualities. Material Memoir is currently on Artiform, Mylapore till October 31. The sculptures are priced at ₹30,000 onwards. Published - October 03, 2026 06:57 pm IST

Of these, 71 had been out of school for one to three years, while another 11 had been out of school for three years or more. IRCDUC said its interventions included helping children re-enter school, facilitating access to documents, and following up with schools and government departments. However, gaps remain. body_clean: The Chennai Port Authority recently launched ‘Port Setu’ to digitise the tracking of export container movement from Container Freight Station (CFS) to Chennai Port. The system was developed by the National Association of Container Freight Stations (NACFS), Chennai Chapter, under the One Nation One Port Process initiative. This is the first phase of the Intelligent Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS), which monitors vehicle movement using Automatic Number Plate Recognition, Optical Character Recognition, RFID readers, and software integration, including Customs’ ICEGATE. The primary advantages of ‘Port Setu’ include digitally recording the transit time of export containers and analysing their actual movements and ground realities, according to a press release. “It provides a common platform for Chennai Customs, Chennai Port Authority, and CFSs to monitor export container movement from CFS Gate-Out to Chennai Port entry and validate transit times against the Customs-prescribed timelines,” it said. It will also improve trailer turnaround time and reduce dependence on manual verification. When phase II of the IVMS is implemented, gate-entry processes at the port will become completely digital. Sachin S. Kurve, Chairperson, Chennai Port Authority, said ‘Port Setu’, implemented by NACFS (Chennai Chapter), will offer better visibility of container movement and help CFSs to optimise trailer management within Chennai Port Authority. M. Periasamy, Commissioner of Customs (Preventive), Chennai Customs, said trailer movement would be streamlined through the digitalisation and automation of procedures, helping Chennai Customs ensure compliance with prescribed procedures. title: Booth-less toll fee collection at Tamil Nadu’s Paranur: how does the multi-lane free flow system work?

summary_clean: The advanced contactless and barrierless tolling system eliminates the need for motor vehicles to stop at toll plazas
body_clean: The Paranur toll plaza on the Chennai-Tiruchi National Highway, on September 30, 2026, became Tamil Nadu’s first booth-less facility to collect toll fee from motor vehicle users through the multi-lane free flow (MLFF) system. MLFF, an advanced contactless and barrierless tolling system, eliminates the need for vehicles to stop at toll plazas by using advanced technologies based on FASTag, radio-frequency identification (RFID) technology, and ANPR technology for seamless electronic toll collection. Why the shift to MLFF? The primary factor is uninterrupted traffic flow. Vehicles no longer need to stop or slow down at toll plazas, thus leading to smoother traffic movement and reduced congestion. Second, operational efficiency and cost savings. Reduced reliance on toll booth infrastructure and manpower results in lower operating costs. And finally, environmental benefits. Smoother traffic flow reduces vehicular idling, cutting down emissions and contributing to cleaner air near tolling points. How does MLFF work? While conventional fee plazas rely on physical booths, gates, and lane infrastructure, under the MLFF system, high-performance RFID readers detect the FASTag affixed on vehicles at high speeds. At the same time, ANPR cameras capture license plate data while radar and LiDAR systems accurately detect and classify vehicles. MLFF equipment creates a toll transaction by reading the FASTag as well as the vehicle number plate and deducts the fee from the FASTag. It also captures evidence of vehicles where payment fails. The MLFF system works across all weather and lighting conditions, round the clock. MLFF thus delivers a fast, transparent, and high-integrity revenue process replacing the traditional toll collection system that cause delays and frustration. What should a vehicle user do? A motor vehicle user travelling on roads should maintain an active FASTag with sufficient balance and ensure that high security registration plates (HSRP) license plates are clearly visible. e-notices Vehicles without the tags or with insufficient balance will be issued challans. If a vehicle fails to pay the applicable user fee while crossing an MLFF plaza, an electronic notice or e-notice shall be issued for recovery of the unpaid fee. As per Rule 14 of the National Highway Fee Determination of Rates and Collection Rules 2008, e-notice will be sent via SMS to the registered mobile number of the vehicle owner, as per Vaahan database, and also to the mobile number linked to the FASTag of the vehicle, as per issuer bank’s records. e-notice amount shall be twice the applicable user fee. However, if payment is made within 72 hours of issuance, a 50% discount shall apply. After 72 hours, the road user shall be required to pay the full e-notice amount. Suspension of FASTag If the road user takes no action within the stipulated time period, related Vaahan services such as No Objection Certificate (NOC), Transfer of Ownership, National Permit, and Fitness Certification will be restricted as per CMVR 1989. Until all e-notices are cleared, the FASTag will remain suspended and will be non-functional at all toll plazas, including State fee plazas and parking facilities across India. e-notice grievance redressal Any aggrieved road user may raise a grievance along with supporting evidence through the National Informatics Centre (NIC) portal within 72 hours of issuance of e-notice, following which the grievance is forwarded to the fee plaza or bank for review and necessary action. The fee plaza will have five days to review the grievance and either accept or reject it. If the fee plaza takes no action within the stipulated time, the claim of the fee plaza to the unpaid user fee shall cease and the grievance will be automatically deemed accepted in favor of road user. If the grievance is accepted, the e-notice will be revoked, but if rejected, the road user shall have to pay the e-notice amount. Road safety measures NHAI’s Project Implementation Unit (PIU) will ensure there is proper illumination at the MLFF equipment location, which will enhance the efficiency of the equipment and associated toll revenue with it. Other road safety aspects like closure of medians, illumination at the existing toll plaza, road marking, and signages, will be thoroughly examined. As the MLFF tolling involves high-speed movement of the vehicles near the MLFF toll plazas as in the case of other sections of the highway, NHAI will ensure the MLFF toll plaza, gantry location, etc., are thoroughly audited by the road safety auditor of the PIU. Their creative association produced some of Tamil cinemaâs most unusual films â stories in which a star could play a blind violinist, perform without dialogue, shrink himself into the unforgettable Appu or multiply into four entirely different men. The researchers assessed the knowledge, attitudes and practices related to haemovigilance among 150 postgraduate doctors. Haemovigilance is a system used to monitor, document and analyse adverse events associated with blood transfusions. Indiaâs programme, launched in 2012, collects information on adverse reactions related to blood transfusions to help hospitals investigate the cause of such reactions, improve transfusion procedures and strengthen patient safety. Both serious and non-serious reactions are meant to be reported. Nearly all participants were aware of different blood components. A similar number identified the blood products used to treat anaemia and thrombocytopenia, or low platelet count. All participants agreed that health institutions should enrol in the haemovigilance programme and report transfusion reactions. About 26%, or 39 of the 150 doctors, said they had formally reported a transfusion reaction, and 21.3%, or about 32 doctors, had attended a haemovigilance-specific education programme or workshop. The study found that, despite familiarity with blood components and transfusion indications, awareness of the national haemovigilance programme and the Transfusion Reaction Reporting Form remained limited. âTheoretical awareness alone is not enough,â said Akilandeeshwari K, the studyâs first author from Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research. Doctors in training are often among the first to assess patients who develop fever, chills, breathing difficulty, rashes or other symptoms during or after a transfusion. Such documentation can help hospitals identify patterns, examine whether an error occurred and prevent recurrence. body_clean: âTt is so quiet out here,â was what one of the hearing impaired participants observed, on taking a walk through Nanmangalam forest. It was 7am and there was just the chirping of birds and insects to be heard. âFor people with hearing impairment who use hearing aids, the urban soundscape can sometimes become overwhelmingly loud,â says Anjana Venkatecan of Care Earth Trust, which collaborated with the Deaf Artists Collective (DFC) to conduct the nature walk recently, along with the Tamil Nadu forest department. âBeing able to access a peaceful place and experience the sounds of nature was a big deal for them,â she says. DFC, a creative community initiative under Madras Photo Bloggers, aims to bridge the accessibility gap by creating meaningful and dignified opportunities for deaf people to explore various spaces. Though they have had photo walks before, this is the first exclusive nature walk for the deaf to be conducted with their communication needs in mind. âWhen it is primarily a photo walk, participants may be more interested in photography than in learning about the environment,â says Anjana. âHaving sign language interpretation and a deaf-friendly environment made it easier for them to participate, learn, connect with others and enjoy the experience without worrying about communication barriers.â Srivatsan Sankaran, founder of Madras Photo Bloggers, says many deaf people do not always get opportunities to experience and capture nature because of communication and accessibility barriers. âMost outdoor activities and nature experiences are designed around hearing-based communication. body_clean: CHENNAI: Residents of Officers Colony in Adambakkam have appealed to the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) to take urgent action against the growing stray dog menace on Daniel Street. Members of the DAM Association report that for over a year, a pack of 7-8 dogs from neighbouring Abraham and Mastan Gori Streets has been gathering at the entrance of Daniel Street around midnight. The howling and aggressive behaviour severely disrupt residents’ sleep and leave pedestrians, delivery personnel, and locals terrified. DAM Association founder R Parthasarathy said that the menace has increased. “Two months ago, a child was bitten in the street and required medical treatment. In the recent months, the stray dogs have killed 4 cats and a hen in the neighbourhood,” he lamented. “These dogs frequently jump compound walls, with one recently jumping onto my parked car; now I stay awake from midnight to 5 am to guard the pets.” R Chandra, a resident of Daniel Street, recounted an incident where three dogs entered her property and attacked her caged pet cat, damaging items spread in the area. Multiple complaints to the 1913 civic helpline resulted in workers capturing the dogs for rabies vaccination and returning them shortly after. “Vaccination does not curb their aggressive behaviour, but officials claim legal limitations prevent further action,” added Parthasarathy. Following Supreme Court directives instructing State governments to shelter aggressive and rabies-affected stray dogs, the GCC began constructing two specialised quarantine facilities in Manali and Perungudi, each designed to house 250 dogs. The construction of these shelters has remained incomplete over a year later. According to GCC, it opened a special quarantine facility in May at Ma Po Si Nagar in Perungudi, which can house 100 dogs with rabies and biting tendencies. With the target of vaccinating 2 lakh stray dogs, GCC began a mass vaccination drive in August. Till September 20, vaccinations have been administered to 86,489 stray dogs across 8 zones. Responding to the issue, GCC Veterinary Officer Kamal Hussain said that officials have been told to catch ferocious dogs on the street and keep them in observation. “Within a week, a quarantine centre with a full capacity of 250 dogs at Manali zone will be inaugurated. In the next month, a centre at Perungudi will be opened with the same capacity,” he explained.

title: Sewage stagnation between railway tracks degrading borewell water, fume Pattabiram residents

body_clean: CHENNAI: Unchecked sewage diversion and severe infrastructure neglect at the Pattabiram railway station have pushed daily rail commuters and residents into a major public health crisis. Untreated household sewage, diverted into storm water drains (SWDs), is continuously stagnating between the two railway tracks adjacent to the station. According to the Rail Passengers Association, stagnant sewage has turned the station premises into a hazardous breeding ground for mosquitoes and poisonous insects. The environmental contamination has severely degraded groundwater quality, making borewell water unsafe and causing widespread skin infections. A Roy Rozario, president of the Rail Passengers Association and a resident of Pattabiram, said, “I’ve sent a formal letter to CM Cell, Southern Railways and Avadi Corporation to divert the SWD to the Railway Road. However, neither Southern Railway, Avadi Corporation, nor defence authorities have taken concrete action in the last four years to construct proper storm drains and reroute sewage along Railway Road. The bureaucratic shuffling between Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) and Avadi Corporation is actively endangering the health and safety of thousands of daily suburban passengers and residents. If an urgent joint inspection is not conducted, we will be constrained to move the National Green Tribunal (NGT) for immediate intervention.” Echoing him, R Adkikesavan, VP of Rail Passengers Association, said that due to the stagnation, borewell water has turned yellow. “While testing the water, lab results revealed that the total dissolved solids are 3 times higher than normal. Often, we get a foul smell in the water,” he added. “We’re unable to rely on groundwater, even while paying tax to the Corporation. We’re forced to purchase drinking water regularly in water cans and tanker lorries. Among residents who live near the railway road, we witness widespread skin diseases.” Since 2009, a scheme to install drinking water supply and sewage infrastructure remains incomplete. However, in the recently concluded assembly session, the TVK government announced a Rs 500 crore project for a 24/7 uninterrupted drinking water supply system in the Avadi Municipal Corporation. Responding to the issue, an official in the Avadi Corporation said, “As the land belongs to the Railways Department, we’ll take further action regarding the re-routing. Also, the encroachments alongside the railways will be removed.” Further, Rozario added, “The Railways department explained that the defence has given the land for use by railways; they do not have the sketch for the area. So he’s unable to move the encroachments.” Attempts to reach a railway official for a comment proved futile.

title: Indigenous tech to determine foetal age in 2027-28, says IIT-Madras

body_clean: CHENNAI: From a Western formula to an India-specific AI model, pregnancy care could be set for a technology shift, with IIT-Madras working towards wider deployment of a home-grown tool to estimate foetal age from ultrasound scans by 2027-28. Prof Balaraman Ravindran, head, Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI, said that the technology, developed using Indian pregnancy data, would be taken through further validation and the next stage of integration with ultrasound scanning systems. In an exclusive interaction with DT Next, he added, “The model seeks to address the limitations of applying formulae developed using Western populations to Indian pregnancies. Currently, they use some US formula to determine the age of the foetus. We’ve developed an Indian babies’ formula.” The India-specific model, Garbhini-GA2, was developed and externally validated using data from Indian pregnancies. Published research has shown that it significantly reduced errors in estimating gestational age compared with the widely used Hadlock formula. The technology was also externally validated using data from Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore. Ravindran stated that the technology had produced “very good results” in work involving CMC Vellore and Faridabad, with the research papers already published. “The focus now is on translating the research into a deployable hospital technology,” he explained. “The technology is all ready. title: T Nagar families caught between patta and NOC in 20-year fight for electricity

body_clean: CHENNAI: For more than 20 years, residents of Thanakottiyammal Thottam and Muthureddy Thottam in T Nagar have been seeking electricity connections, with the status of the land being poromboke leaving several houses without power. This is despite the Tamil Nadu electricity regulations allowing connections to houses on poramboke land under certain conditions. More than 230 families live in the two settlements, which have been occupied for several generations. The demand for electricity came to the fore again on September 9, when more than 50 residents staged a protest outside the substation on Bazullah Road. “We’re asking for electricity for decades, They had provided water and sewer connections but they drew the line on electricity,” said Ravi, a resident from Muthureddy Thottam. “We’re tired of repeated protests.” Residents have been caught in a dispute over the status of the land. When they approached the Revenue Department for an NOC, officials said that the land did not fall under their control and therefore, the NOC could not be issued. When the land was treated as private land, residents were asked to produce patta, they say. Under Regulation 27 (12) of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Distribution Code, electricity can be provided to houses on poramboke land with an NOC from the concerned government authority. Residents have to give an undertaking that the connection does not give them ownership and that they will vacate if the government requires it. “The settlements date back several decades,” said CPM T Nagar Block secretary M Kumar. “Families are said to have been living there since 1935, having migrated from Kancheepuram, Chengalpattu and Tiruvannamalai.” The land, which exceeded the ceiling limit, was acquired by the government under the Land Ceiling Act of 1956. It was not subsequently taken up for development and remained as it was. The Slum Clearance Board declared the area as recognised slum-clearance land in 1972, while a relaxation introduced in 1984 allowed former inhabitants to make claims over the land. Water and sewer connections were also not provided initially, but these were subsequently secured following court proceedings. The electricity issue, however, persisted. A case was filed in 2003 and an order was obtained in 2004, following which electricity was provided to 40 families in February 2005. Meanwhile, the State government is now planning to make it easier for some such houses to get electricity by allowing domestic connections on certain categories of poramboke land without an NOC. But the proposed provision is limited to houses with a built-up area of not more than 250 sq ft. The proposed provision will not cover all categories of poramboke land. Water Course Poramboke, Meikkal, Mandaveli/Meichchal Tharai Poramboke, forest land, railway and other Union government land, patta land belonging to religious institutions and Temple Poramboke land have been excluded.

title: Chennai friends turn shared love for baking into dessert venture Serh

body_clean: CHENNAI: What began in a kitchen, with food being made for friends and family, has now turned into Serh, a new food venture by friends Vritti Miranda and Avantica MP. The duo is bringing together cookies, cheesecakes and cakes, with a menu built around familiar flavours, thoughtful combinations and a little nostalgia. Serh, pronounced from the Tamil word serkkai, meaning to gather or join, is rooted in the duo’s shared love for food and the memories created around a dining table. “Food has always been at the centre of both our families. The best memories happened around a table, especially during festivals and special occasions,” they say. Avantica, fondly known as Akku, has always baked and cooked for friends and family, never imagining she would sell her creations. “A few of us kept telling her she had to share it with more people. She finally agreed, on one condition: I’d handle the business, logistics and numbers, and she’d be free to do what she does best: create. That’s really how Serh was born,” says Vritti. The cookie menu currently features The OG, Hella Nella, Dark AF, Campfire, Nuttin’ But Toffee, Periya Pista, Ruby Ripple and Golden Hour. The duo says they experimented with more than 60 flavour combinations before narrowing down the final selection. We sampled The OG, Hella Nella, Ruby Ripple and Golden Hour, and each had its own character. The OG, the first cookie Akku made for Serh, is a classic chocolate chip cookie with crisp edges and a gooey centre. Hella Nella combines Nutella, hazelnut and dark chocolate, while Ruby Ripple pairs raspberry with white chocolate. The standout for us was Golden Hour, which brings together Biscoff, white chocolate and pecans. The pecans add a nutty edge that balances the sweetness of the Biscoff. The cheesecakes follow the New York style, with berry, salted caramel and Biscoff toppings. Getting the texture right took more than 10 trials, with the duo settling on a dense yet creamy cheesecake with a buttery biscuit crunch. Philadelphia cream cheese is used to achieve the desired richness. Then comes the Old School cake, available in chocolate and raspberry-strawberry buttercream versions. We tried the chocolate variant, and it immediately brought back memories of school-time bakery cakes and birthday celebrations. Made with a soft yellow cake and semi-sweet chocolate buttercream, it has that familiar homemade quality while being less sweet than traditional versions. For Serh, the idea is not to be restricted to just desserts. “We don’t really see ourselves as a home bakery or a dessert brand. We’re two friends who want to do food right and keep it simple, uncomplicated and delicious,” says Vritti. Serh launched at The Vizha Pop-up by Madras Finds on September 5 and 6, selling out on both days. Customer feedback has since led to the addition of Dark AF, a 70 per cent dark chocolate and sea salt cookie. The duo is currently setting up its cloud kitchen in Chetpet and operates on a pre-order basis, with deliveries on Fridays and Saturdays for now. Once the kitchen is fully functional, they plan to deliver throughout the week. The menu will also gradually expand into savoury offerings.

body_clean: CHENNAI: What began as a biodiversity walk with children has evolved into Imago-1, an international exhibition featuring young artists between the ages of nine and 20. Curated by Diana R, founder of Diana’s Art Room Studios and artist and sculptor M Vennimalai, the exhibition explores ‘Patterns in Nature’ through paintings, installations, woodwork, leather works and other mediums. The three-month project began when the Madras Crocodile Bank Trust’s Nature Education and Conservation division, Nature Ed, approached Diana with a proposal for a biodiversity walk. Instead of treating it as a one-day field trip, Diana wanted the children to take what they observed back to the studio and develop it into an exhibition. “We went on a biodiversity walk with the Nature Ed team. The children walked into the Irular settlement across the bank, and we saw tessellated scales on snake skin, ladybugs, turtle shells, red chameleon, birds, insects and many more things. The children started observing the patterns in nature. We brought those observations back into the art studio and took the learning further,” says Diana. The children then explored ideas such as MC Escher’s tessellations, fractals, mathematical patterns in art, bioluminescent ecosystems, conservation and wildlife. What started as an observation exercise gradually became a deeper exploration of how patterns occur in the natural world. “It became a very big learning experience for the children and me. Rather than asking the children to reproduce what they had seen, I encouraged them to interpret the ideas that resonated with them. The result was a collection of works that reflect their individual observations and approaches,” adds the curator. One student collected real termite wings and made an installation. She spent 30 hours working on it, says Diana. The exhibition brings together works in different mediums, textures and forms, including canvas, installations, wood and leather. Around 90 per cent of the works are by students of Diana’s Art Room in Adyar, while the remaining works are by young artists who responded to an international open call. The call received entries from Singapore and Russia, as well as different parts of Tamil Nadu. Noushad Ali, a resident of Ayodhya Colony in Velachery, was constructing a new house where more than ten labourers from Bihar and Odisha were working. On Saturday morning, co-workers found Ranjan (35) from Odisha lying dead on the first floor with stab injuries. They immediately alerted police, after which a team rushed to the scene and sent Ranjan's body to the Royapettah GH. A probe found that Ranjan had a monetary dispute with three other workers from Bihar -- Kasim (26), Tabir (28), and Sharipul (30). Police said an argument broke out between them on Friday night, after which the three of them allegedly attacked Ranjan with a knife and fled the spot after killing him. Velachery Police have formed special teams to trace the suspects.

title: Chennai Corporation prepared to handle northeast monsoon, says Commissioner Sameeran
title_clean: Chennai Corporation prepared to handle northeast monsoon, says Commissioner Sameeran
title_normalized: chennai corporation prepared to handle northeast monsoon says commissioner sameeran
body_clean: CHENNAI: The Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) is prepared to handle the northeast monsoon, with precautionary measures being taken across the city, Corporation Commissioner GS Sameeran said on Saturday. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the northeast monsoon is expected to set in between October 15 and 20. Sameeran said the civic body was also preparing for the possibility of extreme rainfall of 20 to 30 cm in a single day due to cloudbursts, depressions or cyclones. Inspecting the double-vent stormwater drain project at Tidel Park in Taramani, Sameeran said the project would improve flood mitigation in the IIT Madras campus, spread over nearly 610 acres, and the adjoining Guindy National Park, including the Lok Bhavan premises. The GCC had taken up the project based on past incidents and a technical committee's recommendations. The double-vent cut-and-cover drain extends 660 metres from its starting point to the South Buckingham Canal through the Open Space Reservation (OSR) area of Tidel Park and will discharge stormwater into the canal. The project has been divided into two packages. Package 1 comprises a 330-metre cut-and-cover drain, of which work on 40 metres is expected to be finished within 10 days. Package 2 involves a complex 90-metre stretch across OMR near the CMRL underground station. It includes a 45-metre CMRL segment and night-time work on OMR, which is awaiting police clearance. The package is expected to be completed within 20 days. Across the city, short-term and medium-term flood mitigation works are nearing completion. Of the 1,600 km of stormwater drains, 1,400 km have been desilted and works on 200 km are expected to be completed in a week. The second round of cleaning is under way across all 1.1 lakh silt catch pits. The GCC has deployed heavy machinery, including robotic excavators and amphibious machines, to clear critical culverts along Radial Road, railway lines and the Virugambakkam Canal, which is to be completed by October 15. In coordination with the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), around 70 per cent of temporary access structures and boulders obstructing the Cooum have been removed. Complete removal is targeted by mid-October. The civic body has prepared 215 relief centres and 111 community kitchens and stocked emergency kits with essential supplies, including rice, milk powder and sanitary napkins. More than 5,200 volunteers have registered through the Namma Chennai app to assist with relief and medical operations. As part of measures to improve road safety, the GCC has banned new road cuts except for emergency repairs. It has allocated Rs 29 crore for pre-monsoon patchwork. The Metro Water Board has been asked to pay Rs 120 crore towards restoring roads damaged by cuts in south Chennai. The GCC also said complaints received through its 1913 helpline would be addressed within 72 hours.

A total of 322 people, including 310 passengers and 12 crew members, were on board. All the passengers had boarded the aircraft and the doors had been closed when the pilot detected a technical snag as the aircraft began moving along the runway. The pilot immediately brought the aircraft to a stop and alerted the Chennai airport control room. The aircraft was subsequently towed back to its departure point. Passengers were asked to disembark while a team of aircraft engineers inspected the plane and worked to rectify the technical snag. The passengers were later transported in buses to various hotels in Chennai for accommodation. The airline has announced that the flight is expected to depart for Singapore tonight after the technical snag is rectified. All 322 people on board, including 310 passengers, were safe.

body_clean: CHENNAI: The need for early diagnosis of brachial plexus injuries, including in patients with head injuries, was stressed at a Continuing Medical Education (CME) programme organised by the Institute for Research and Rehabilitation of Hand and the Department of Plastic Surgery, Government Stanley Medical College and Hospital, here. The programme, held in the campus last week to commemorate World Hand Surgery Day observed on August 23, focused on distinguishing brachial plexus injuries from other nerve injuries of the upper limb. Experts stressed that early identification and appropriate intervention could help expedite recovery. Dr Sabari Girish Ambat, consultant, Apollo First Med Hospital, Chennai, spoke on ‘Diagnosing Brachial Plexus Injuries – Clinical Pearls and Tricks’, while Dr Sivakumar A, Consultant, Desire Aesthetics, Chennai, discussed upper-limb microvascular surgery, including emergency revascularisation and replantation. The sessions also covered techniques to salvage and restore hand function in trauma, tumours and congenital upper-limb conditions. Conducted in hybrid mode, the CME enabled postgraduate students and trainees from other institutions to participate in the academic discussions. Prof Dr A Aravind, Dean, Government Stanley Medical College; Dr S Jothikumar, Medical Superintendent; Dr B Vanithamalar, RMO; and Dr G S Radhakrishnan, Head, Department of Plastic Surgery and others attended the event.

body_clean: CHENNAI: Residents of Srinivasapuram in Pattinapakkam are living in fear as several Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board (TNUHDB) tenements are in a damaged condition. There are a total of 1,536 houses in the area. With the monsoon season underway, residents fear that the weakened structures may collapse and have urged the authorities to provide alternative houses at the earliest. Residents said that a survey has been conducted to identify the damaged houses and the process of providing alternative houses to those living in them is underway. However, they said there has been a delay in shifting residents from the damaged buildings. The ceilings, balconies and staircases of several houses have been damaged. Residents are afraid to stay inside their homes and use common areas. They have urged the authorities to provide alternative houses before the damaged structures deteriorate further during the rainy season and pose a risk to residents. A resident, Usharani, said, “It’s frightening to live in the house. Parts of the house, both inside and outside, could collapse at any time. The ceiling inside is also damaged and broken. We’re scared even while sleeping and eating. The staircases and balconies, which are used for safety and access, are also damaged. We’re living in fear every day.” Another resident, Selvam, said, “We’ve been living in this area with our family for the past 40 years. When our children were studying at home, a portion of the building collapsed near them. Since then, we have been afraid to stay inside the house. As the rainy season has started, the damaged buildings could become weaker and collapse. As per the scheme guidelines, land cannot be provided separately and houses have to be constructed and allotted to beneficiaries. The Chief Engineer is visit the area tomorrow, officials said.

body_clean: CHENNAI: Government exam aspirants and readers from districts outside Chennai are facing difficulties in obtaining membership at the Anna Centenary Library due to the existing requirement for address attestation by a Notary Public, prompting students to seek a simpler Aadhaar-based registration process. The Anna Centenary Library, one of the city’s major public knowledge hubs, has become a popular destination for competitive examination aspirants, research scholars and readers seeking a conducive environment for reading and self earning. However, readers from other districts said that the membership procedure has become a hurdle, particularly for those without a Chennai address proof. Those having a regional address at Chennai or Kancheepuram, Tiruvallur, Chengalpattu (KTCC) can obtain library membership by submitting Aadhaar or other government issued identity documents carrying their address. But, readers from other districts are required to provide an ‘address accreditation’ certificate attested by a Notary Public for membership. Raja, a library member from a Delta district, said the annual membership fee was only Rs 200, but obtaining the required address attestation had cost him Rs 500. “Some people have reportedly paid around Rs 2,000 to get the address certificate from a Notary Public. It is unreasonable to spend several times the annual membership fee merely to complete the address verification process,” he lamented. Government exam aspirant Kayalvizhi said that the Anna Centenary Library had become a major support system for aspirants from across Tamil Nadu. “The library is a boon for those of us preparing for competitive exams. Aspirants from different parts of the State come here to prepare for various exams. The library also provides a good ecosystem where we can meet senior aspirants and learn from their experiences,” she said. Kayalvizhi pointed out that many aspirants from other districts stay in hostels, paying guest accommodation or bachelor rooms in and around Chennai, and therefore do not possess a local address proof. “I stay in a hostel in Tambaram. Without library membership, I cannot access the book lending facility. If I need a book for my preparation, I have to travel to the library every day just to read it,” she said. Aspirants have urged the library administration to simplify the procedure and allow readers from all districts to obtain membership using Aadhaar or any other valid government issued identity document, similar to the procedure followed for Chennai-based applicants.

body_clean: CHENNAI: The State Highways Department’s Rs 48-crore project to widen Sardar Patel Road from Highway Research Station to Anna University has reached 50% completion, with the shifting of high-tension cables emerging as a key reason for the delay. The widening work between Anna University and Madhya Kailash has been completed. Permission has been sought from the National Green Tribunal (NGT) for cutting trees in Guindy Nation Park to widen the stretch between the Cancer Institute and the Park, while widening work near Gandhi Mandapam is progressing. Meanwhile, arches built for Gandhi Jayanthi and Kamarajar’s death anniversary on October 2 are yet to be removed. Officials said that the structures would be cleared in the coming days, allowing roadwork in the stretch to resume. “After the cable-shifting work is finished, we’ll take up the alignment of the median along with the lights. We’re working to complete the project as early as possible,” the official said. A TNPDCL official told DT Next that the shifting of the Ring Main Unit (RMU) is scheduled for Saturday. “The shifting will be taken up tomorrow and the work will be completed in 1-2 days,” the official said. Residents, however, expressed concern over the slow progress on the arterial road, which serves several important institutions and landmarks, including educational institutions, Guindy National Park, Gandhi Mandapam, the Kamarajar Memorial and Lok Bhavan. “The progress is barely noticeable, yet hundreds of vehicles pass through here during peak hours. In the morning and evening, traffic from Rajiv Gandhi Salai piles up from the IIT Madras campus to the intersection of Gandhi Mandapam Road and Sardar Patel Road. With the monsoon around the corner, we urge officials to complete the work on time,” said Pushpa Raj, a resident of West Canal Bank Road in Kotturpuram.

Damage to the railway property has been a recurring issue, and we’re planning to create awareness among the public. We’ll also intensify vigilance to curb such activities.”

title: FOMRRA petitions NPCI, Fin Min for Rs 5 UPI merchant discount rate on maintenance collections
title_clean: FOMRRA petitions NPCI, Fin Min for Rs 5 UPI merchant discount rate on maintenance collections

body_clean: CHENNAI: The Federation of OMR Residents Associations (FOMRRA), representing over 250 gated communities along the city’s IT Corridor, OMR, has partnered with community governance platform ADDA (3Five8 Technologies) to submit a formal joint representation to the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) and the Ministry of Finance. Supported by a national coalition of nearly 200,000 Resident Welfare Associations (RWAs), including MahaSewa, the Bangalore Apartments Federation (BAF), and Chandivali Citizens Welfare Association (CCWA), the petition urges the government to notify apartment maintenance collections as an essential utility category eligible for a flat Rs 5 Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions above Rs 2,000. The coalition strongly opposes the proposed 0.4 per cent commercial MDR levy set to take effect on 15 October. The petition highlights that housing communities operate strictly on a non-profit, cost-recovery basis, collecting funds solely to pay for shared essential services such as security, water, common-area electricity, and lift maintenance. While direct payments to power and water utilities already qualify for the flat Rs 5 MDR rate, aggregating these payments through an RWA penalises citizens with a 0.4% fee. On a standard maintenance bill of Rs 10,000, this extracts Rs 40 per flat, eight times the utility rate, whereas on quarterly bills of Rs 25,000, the fee jumps to Rs 100 per transaction. This charge will ultimately be passed back to residents as higher maintenance costs, violating the core principle that consumers should not bear UPI charges. “Applying a commercial 0.4% MDR on housing society maintenance is fundamentally irrational. RWAs do not retain trade margins or earn profits, warning that imposing commercial charges will force honorary, voluntary resident committees back to physical cheques, cash collections, and manual bank transfers,” stated Harsha Koda, co-founder of FOMRRA. “This threatens years of hard-won digital adoption, increases administrative chaos and disrupts statutory audits.” The coalition also criticised broader regulatory misunderstandings, such as the 18% GST on maintenance fees above Rs 7,500, urging the government to stop treating non-profit communities as commercial businesses. Key demands include a dedicated Merchant Category Code (MCC) for registered RWAs and an immediate executive notification of the flat Rs 5 UPI rate before October 15.

body_clean: CHENNAI: Dengue cases in Chennai more than doubled in September, with 1,290 infections reported during the month against 605 in August, while 72 fresh cases were detected on Wednesday, amid a seasonal rise in vector-borne diseases across Tamil Nadu. The sharp increase comes as the State steps up surveillance and vector-control measures ahead of the northeast monsoon. Tamil Nadu had recorded more than 18,000 dengue cases and nine deaths up to September 30, according to the Health and Family Welfare Department. Chennai was among the districts identified as having a high incidence of dengue. The Health Department has intensified fever surveillance and field-level interventions. As of September 30, fever monitoring was being carried out at 5,818 government and private health facilities, with 26,303 health workers deployed for surveillance and rapid-response activities. More than 2.23 lakh dengue-related tests had also been conducted during the first nine months of the year. The Greater Chennai Corporation has deployed 3,690 domestic breeding checkers across its 15 zones to identify and eliminate mosquito-breeding sites. Authorities have also intensified source-reduction activities, cleaning and fogging operations, particularly in areas reporting higher incidence. Health officials have urged residents to remove stagnant water from homes and surroundings, regularly clean flower pots and containers, and keep stored water covered to prevent aedes mosquito breeding. Hospitals are also strengthening preparedness by earmarking extra beds for dengue patients, with mosquito-netted beds and adequate stocks of medicines, intravenous fluids, plasma and blood components. Doctors have advised people with high-grade or persistent fever to seek medical evaluation promptly, particularly as the critical phase of dengue can begin after the fever subsides.
